questions.q: What should the goal of an argument be, according to the summary?
a: Winning your audience over to a shared outcome
Proving that your opponent is factually wrong
Ending the conversation as quickly as possible
Getting the last word before you walk away
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the aim is consensus, not victory, so the audience ends up wanting the same thing.

questions.q: What separated couples who stayed married from those who broke up?
a: They resolved disputes by reaching a shared outcome
They had far fewer disagreements overall
They avoided discussing money and family
They took turns letting each other win
questions.why: Lesson 1 cites Gottman’s finding that both groups argued equally, but only one resolved things.

questions.q: In Aristotle’s scheme, which tense matches an argument about blame?
a: The past
The present
The future
The conditional
questions.why: Lesson 2 pairs blame with the past, values with the present and choice with the future.

questions.q: How could the wife keep the music dispute about choice rather than values?
a: By asking whether they could turn it down or switch songs
By explaining why her taste in music is superior
By pointing out that he always plays it too loud
By refusing to discuss the music until later
questions.why: Lesson 2 recommends focusing on the future with a question about what they might do instead.

questions.q: What does the summary suggest doing when an opponent insults you?
a: Embrace the label and give it a positive spin
Insult them back with a sharper word
Ignore them and repeat your main point
End the discussion and walk away
questions.why: Lesson 3 shows how redefining a label, as politicians do, puts the opponent on the defensive.
